candidates: When a useEffect registers window-level event listeners (mousemove, mouseup, etc.) inside a nested callback (e.g., an onStart handler spawned from a mousedown), the effect's cleanup function must also remove those nested window listeners. Only cleaning up the directly-registered listeners leaves orphaned handlers if the component unmounts mid-interaction.

Utility functions that cycle or index into a collection must handle the empty-collection edge case explicitly. If the stated return type is non-nullable (e.g., `string`) but `Object.keys(map).length` could be 0, add an early guard that returns a safe sentinel or throws a descriptive error rather than silently returning `undefined`.

Use named module-level constants instead of repeating their raw values as inline literals. When constants like `VIEWPORT_MIN_WIDTH` and `VIEWPORT_MIN_HEIGHT` are already defined in the same file, reference them everywhere—including inside callbacks—so that a single change to the constant propagates everywhere.

Avoid TypeScript non-null assertions (`!`) on properties that the interface declares as optional (`?`). When a `Viewport`-style interface marks `type` as `type?: ViewportType`, accessing `value.type!` silently breaks on user-provided objects that omit the field. Provide an explicit fallback (e.g., `value.type ?? 'other'`) instead.

Do not use `.replace('px', '')` to extract numeric values from CSS dimension strings. This silently produces wrong results for non-pixel units (`%`, `em`, `rem`, `vw`, `vh`). Use `parseFloat()` or a regex that strips any trailing unit characters (e.g., `/[a-z%]+$/i`) so all unit types are handled correctly.

After refactoring a component to use shared library components (e.g., replacing bespoke styled wrappers with ActionList), remove every import that is no longer referenced in the file. Stale imports (e.g., leftover `darken`, `transparentize`, or `styled`) create false dependency signals and will trigger lint/compiler warnings.

Do not declare props in a styled component's generic type parameter unless the styling function actually reads and applies them. A prop like `muted?: boolean` that is declared but never used in the styles creates dead API surface: callers pass it expecting an effect, but nothing happens. Either wire the prop into the style logic or remove it from the type.

When renaming a DOM element's `id` (or the selector used to query it), search the entire codebase for every consumer of the old ID—`querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` calls, `href` skip-link anchors, `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` attributes, and tests—and update them all in the same commit. Partial migrations silently break features such as skip navigation.

When replacing a bespoke styled component with a shared design-system component, visually verify that all interactive states (focus ring offset, hover background, active color) still match the surrounding UI. Shared components may default to a different `outline-offset`, `border-radius`, or `background` than what was previously hardcoded, causing subtle visual regressions.

Every `<input>` element must have an associated `<label>` element linked via a stable ID. Use `useId` (e.g., from `@react-aria/utils`) to generate a unique ID and pass it to both the `htmlFor` attribute of the label and the `id` attribute of the input. Unlabeled inputs are a WCAG 2.1 Level A violation and will be flagged by accessibility audits.

Render purely decorative characters (colons, slashes, separators) via CSS `content` on a `::before`/`::after` pseudo-element rather than as HTML text nodes. Text-node decorators are announced by screen readers and braille displays, adding noise without conveying meaning. If the character is truly cosmetic, use CSS or omit it entirely.

When a toolbar or canvas control's state is externally locked (e.g., overridden by story globals or parameters), every interactive control that would mutate that state—buttons, text inputs, select dropdowns—must be visually disabled (`disabled` attribute or `aria-disabled`) and reject interaction. A control that accepts input but silently does nothing is both a misleading UX and an accessibility failure.

When a preset-selection dropdown coexists with freeform value inputs (e.g., a viewport picker alongside width/height fields), the dropdown must expose a distinct 'Custom' or equivalent state that activates whenever the user overrides the preset. Without it, simply focusing or opening the dropdown can silently discard the user's custom values.

Toolbar addons and canvas-level UI that are only meaningful in story mode must gate their rendering on `viewMode`. Rendering addon controls in docs mode (or other non-story contexts) where they have no effect produces confusing, non-functional UI. Check `viewMode` before rendering mode-specific components.

Name component props after what the data semantically *is* (e.g., `aside`, `extra`, `secondary`) rather than where it visually *appears* (e.g., `right`, `trailing`, `end`). Visual layout can change across redesigns, but the underlying data model should not; positional names become misleading after any layout change.
